faq.title: Can a buyer on Cashify or OLX recover my deleted photos using software after a standard factory reset?
faq.description: On any modern Android device running Android 10 or later, file-based encryption (FBE) is enforced by hardware. When you initiate a factory reset, Android discards and overwrites the hardware AES-256 decryption keys stored inside the secure element (TEE/Titan M). Without those keys, even state-level forensic tools like Cellebrite or Magnet AXIOM recover only unreadable cryptographic noise.

faq.title: What is Factory Reset Protection (FRP) and why does it cause buyers to reject traded-in phones?
faq.description: Google FRP is an anti-theft security mechanism. If you factory reset a phone without first manually removing your Google Account from Settings, the phone locks itself upon restart and demands your old Gmail password to activate. Cashify inspectors or Amazon exchange agents will immediately fail the trade-in inspection and reject your handset if FRP is triggered.

faq.title: Do I need to overwrite flash memory with zeros like older hard drives (DoD 5220.22-M)?
faq.description: Modern solid-state flash memory (UFS 3.1, UFS 4.0) uses wear-leveling algorithms that make traditional multi-pass zero-fill utilities ineffective and needlessly destructive to flash endurance. Cryptographic erasure (Crypto-Erase / NIST SP 800-88) is the internationally recognized gold standard for flash memory sanitization.

html:
The Hidden Peril of the Second-Hand Smartphone Market

Trading in your old smartphone through exchange programs on platforms like Cashify, Amazon India, Flipkart, or local repair shops has become standard practice when upgrading to a new handset. The transaction is swift: an inspection agent evaluates your screen condition, cameras, and battery health, offers a quote, and carries your old device away.

However, what happens to the confidential data stored on your phone's internal flash storage? Over years of ownership, your smartphone served as the physical repository for your most sensitive digital assets: banking statements, Aadhaar and PAN scans, private family photos, saved browser credentials, WhatsApp voice notes, and cryptographic two-factor backup tokens. Many users simply navigate to Settings, tap 'Factory data reset', and hand over their phone. Unfortunately, failing to follow a rigorous sanitization protocol can expose you to two catastrophic outcomes: either your private files are recovered by downstream second-hand buyers using consumer forensic software, or the phone triggers Google Factory Reset Protection (FRP), causing the trade-in agent to reject your handset and cancel your trade-in discount.

This comprehensive technical guide outlines the exact, forensic-grade sanitization workflow compliant with NIST SP 800-88 (Guidelines for Media Sanitization) to ensure that your device is 100% unrecoverable while guaranteeing a flawless exchange inspection.

Understanding Android's Cryptographic Storage Architecture

To wipe a smartphone securely, you must understand how modern Android stores files. In the legacy era of Android 4 and 5, smartphones stored user data in plaintext on ext4 partitions. Performing a standard factory reset merely unlinked the file directory indices without erasing the underlying NAND flash memory cells, allowing cheap recovery tools (such as DiskDigger or Recuva) to easily reconstruct deleted JPEG photos and SMS databases.

Beginning with Android 7 and made strictly mandatory on all hardware shipping with Android 10 and later, Google enforced File-Based Encryption (FBE). Under FBE:

  • Every single file on your smartphone is encrypted with its own unique AES-256-XTS symmetric key.
  • These individual file keys are encrypted by a Master Device Key, which is derived from your lock screen passcode (PIN, pattern, or password).
  • The master encryption keys are housed inside a hardware-isolated, tamper-resistant cryptographic co-processor known as the Trusted Execution Environment (TEE) or dedicated security chips (such as Google's Titan M2, Samsung Knox Vault, or Qualcomm Secure Processing Unit).

When you execute an authentic factory reset on an encrypted Android device, the operating system executes a Cryptographic Erasure (Crypto-Erase): it physically destroys the master hardware encryption keys inside the secure enclave. Even if forensic technicians physically desolder the NAND flash memory chip and read every raw bit using specialized chip-off hardware, the extracted payload is mathematically indistinguishable from random white noise. Without the destroyed hardware key, decrypting the photos would require billions of years of supercomputer time.

Step 1: The Critical Prerequisite — Disarming Google FRP & OEM Accounts

The single most common mistake made by sellers is triggering Factory Reset Protection (FRP). If you reset your phone through recovery mode or without properly signing out of accounts, Android assumes the phone was stolen. When the Cashify agent attempts to configure the device, the setup wizard will display: 'This device was reset. To continue, sign in with a Google Account that was previously synced on this device.' If you cannot provide the password, the trade-in is cancelled on the spot.

The Mandatory Account Removal Checklist:

  1. Remove All Google Accounts:
    • Open Settings > Accounts and backup > Manage accounts (or Settings > Passwords & accounts).
    • Tap on your primary Google Account.
    • Tap Remove account and confirm the action.
    • Repeat this step for every secondary Google Account listed on the device.
  2. Sign Out of OEM Manufacturer Cloud Accounts:
    • Samsung Galaxy: Go to Settings > Samsung account (top banner) > Sign out. Enter your Samsung password to deactivate Find My Mobile.
    • Xiaomi / Redmi / POCO: Go to Settings > Mi Account > Sign out. Select 'Turn off Find device' and enter your Mi Account password.
    • OnePlus / Realme / OPPO: Go to Settings > HeyTap / OnePlus Account > Sign out.
    • Apple iPhone (if trading across OS): Go to Settings > Apple ID > Sign Out > Turn off Find My.
  3. Remove the Lock Screen Security Passcode:
    • Go to Settings > Lock screen > Screen lock type.
    • Enter your current PIN or password.
    • Select None (or Swipe) and accept the prompt to remove saved biometric fingerprints and face data. Removing the lock screen PIN before resetting ensures that hardware encryption keys are cleanly disarmed.

Step 2: Performing the Primary Factory Data Reset

Once accounts and passcodes are completely removed, initiate the native factory reset through the user settings menu (never use the bootloader recovery menu when preparing for sale, as recovery menu resets automatically arm FRP):

  1. Ensure your device battery has at least 50% charge or plug it into a wall charger. (A power failure during flash erasure can permanently brick the motherboard).
  2. Navigate to the reset menu:
    • Samsung Galaxy: Settings > General management > Reset > Factory data reset.
    • Google Pixel / Motorola / Nothing: Settings > System > Reset options > Erase all data (factory reset).
    • Xiaomi / POCO: Settings > About phone > Factory reset > Erase all data.
    • OnePlus / Realme: Settings > Additional settings > Back up and reset > Reset phone > Erase all data.
  3. Review the warning list of apps and storage directories that will be purged.
  4. Tap Erase all data / Reset.
  5. The phone will reboot into its kernel recovery partition, execute the cryptographic key destruction and flash block format, and reboot into the out-of-the-box 'Welcome' setup wizard.

Step 3: The Paranoid Protocol — Zero-Fill Overwrite Technique

For 99.9% of users, the native cryptographic erasure executed in Step 2 is mathematically irreversible. However, if your smartphone contains ultra-confidential intellectual property, military records, or high-risk banking keys—or if your device is an older model (running Android 8 or 9) where File-Based Encryption was not universally enforced—you can execute the Dummy Overwrite Protocol to guarantee absolute physical data destruction:

  1. After the phone reboots into the 'Welcome' setup screen, complete the initial setup wizard without connecting to Wi-Fi or entering any Google account. (Skip every prompt, skip adding a PIN, and skip cloud backups).
  2. Launch the Camera application.
  3. Switch to Video mode and set the resolution to maximum (4K UHD at 60 FPS or 1080p).
  4. Place your smartphone flat on a desk with the camera lenses facing a dark mousepad or tabletop (so it records a blank, dark feed).
  5. Hit Record and allow the video recording to run continuously until internal storage is 100% saturated and the camera displays: 'Storage Full — Recording Stopped'.
  6. Why this works: Modern flash controllers write the gigantic multi-gigabyte video stream across all unallocated flash memory blocks, physically overwriting every previously deleted data sector with meaningless black video bits.
  7. Finally, navigate back to Settings and perform a second Factory Data Reset to wipe the dummy video. At this stage, even government-level laboratory electron-microscope analysis cannot retrieve a single byte of your original personal data.

Step 4: Physical Preparations for Maximum Trade-In Value

Now that your data is forensically obliterated, maximize your Cashify or Amazon trade-in payout with these physical verification checks:

Inspection Component What the Agent Checks Preparation Advice
SIM Card & MicroSD Trays Presence of foreign cards or stuck trays Eject physical nano-SIM cards and remove your MicroSD expansion card
Display Oleophobic Coating Scratches, cracks, dead pixels, and screen burn-in Clean screen with an isopropyl alcohol wipe; remove scratched plastic screen guards
Camera Lenses Dust, lens delamination, and autofocus motor Clean lens glass with microfiber; test 1x, 3x, and ultra-wide sensor focus
Microphone & Speakers Distortion or muffled audio playback Use a dry soft toothbrush to gently clean speaker grilles of accumulated pocket lint
IMEI Verification Matches invoice / bill of sale Keep the original box or dial *#06# to display dual IMEI numbers cleanly

What About MicroSD Cards and eSIMs?

Never hand over a smartphone with an active eSIM or forgotten MicroSD card:

  • Physical MicroSD Cards: Always eject the MicroSD card. If you plan to sell the MicroSD card alongside the phone, plug it into a computer and format it using SD Card Formatter with full 'Overwrite Format' enabled.
  • Embedded SIMs (eSIM): During the factory reset process, modern Android will ask: 'Do you want to erase eSIMs?' Ensure you select 'Erase eSIM'. Before erasing, ensure you have contacted your telecom operator (Jio, Airtel, Vi) to transfer the eSIM profile to your new device.

Post-Reset Verification: The Forensic Validation Check

Before handing your phone over to the inspection agent, execute a 60-second verification check to ensure that File-Based Encryption keys are truly destroyed and that no residual account tokens remain:

  1. Verify the 'Welcome' Setup Wizard: On the rebooted screen, select your language, tap Start, and tap Skip on the Wi-Fi connection prompt. If the phone allows you to skip Wi-Fi without displaying an FRP warning modal, the device is completely disarmed and ready for exchange.
  2. Verify Storage State via ADB (Optional for Enthusiasts): If you want absolute cryptographic confirmation, connect the phone to your PC, open a command prompt, and run adb shell df -h. You will observe that the /data user partition is mounted with fresh ext4 or F2FS filesystem superblocks with 100% clean inode pointers.
